caption:
Who discovered Machu Picchu?

In July 1911 the American historian Hiram Bingham III was led up a ridge above the Urubamba River by a local farmer, Melchor Arteaga. Near the top he found a hut with two Quechua families, Richarte and Alvarez, who had cleared and been farming the Inca terraces for four years. Richarte's 11-year-old son Pablito walked Bingham to the main ruins.

Inside the Temple of the Three Windows, Bingham found a name written in charcoal on the central window: "A. Lizárraga 1902". The Peruvian explorer Agustín Lizárraga had cut his way in nine years earlier. Bingham photographed the inscription and published it. In his pocket field journal he wrote that Lizárraga was the discoverer of Machu Picchu. In his last book, Lost City of the Incas (1952), he claimed the find himself.

The city was never truly lost. Maps reference it as early as 1874, and a 1904 atlas labels it Huayna Picchu. Local people knew it, walked to it, farmed it.

In 1912, 1914 and 1915 Bingham removed thousands of artifacts to Yale — ceramics, silver figures, jewellery, human bones — supposedly for 18 months. The final batch went home to Peru in November 2012.

Still open: no contemporary written records confirm what the site was for, and none of Bingham's own hypotheses have been substantiated. A 2021 study argues the builders' name for it was probably Huayna Picchu, or simply Picchu — and that "Machu Picchu" stuck because of Bingham's 1911 publications.

Images: Allard Schmidt, 2005; H. L. Tucker, 1911; Hiram Bingham III, 1911 and 1912; WMrapids, 2021.
